name: git commit
shortDescription: Record changes to the repository. A commit is a permanent snapshot of your staged changes along with a message describing what changed and why.
detailedDescription:
A commit is the fundamental unit of Git history. Each commit records: a snapshot of all staged files, the author's name and email, a timestamp, a commit message, and a pointer to its parent commit(s). Together, these form an immutable chain — the project's complete history.

Commits are identified by a SHA-1 hash (e.g., `a1b2c3d`), which is computed from the commit's content. This means two identical commits always have the same hash, and any tampering with history changes all subsequent hashes.

**Writing good commit messages** is critical. A well-written message explains the *why* behind a change, not just the *what*. The conventional format is: a short summary line (50 chars max), a blank line, then a detailed body explaining the reasoning. Teams often enforce commit message conventions like Conventional Commits (`feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`, etc.).

Commits are cheap and local — they don't touch the remote server until you explicitly push. Commit early and commit often.

parameters.description: Use the given string as the commit message. If omitted, Git opens your configured editor for you to type the message. You can use multiple -m flags for multi-paragraph messages.
Automatically stage all modified and deleted tracked files before committing. Does NOT include new untracked files. A shortcut that skips the separate `git add` step for known files.

Replace the last commit with a new one, combining the previous commit's changes with any newly staged changes. The old commit is discarded. Never amend commits that have been pushed to a shared remote.
Used with --amend. Keeps the original commit message unchanged. Perfect for adding a forgotten file to the last commit without editing the message.
Create a commit even if there are no staged changes. Useful for triggering CI/CD pipelines, marking milestones, or creating merge boundary commits.
Sign the commit with your GPG key to cryptographically prove authorship. Some organizations require signed commits for compliance.
Create a fixup commit for a specified commit. When later running `git rebase --autosquash`, fixup commits are automatically squashed into their target commits.

examples.title: Basic commit with inline message
examples.description: The everyday commit command. Stage your changes first, then commit with a descriptive message.
examples.code:
git add .
git commit -m "Add user login validation"

# Output:
# [main a1b2c3d] Add user login validation
#  3 files changed, 45 insertions(+), 12 deletions(-)

examples.title: Stage and commit tracked files in one step
examples.description: The -a flag automatically stages modified/deleted tracked files. Saves a step, but be careful — it won't pick up new files.
examples.code:
git commit -am "Fix header alignment on mobile"

# Equivalent to:
# git add -u
# git commit -m "Fix header alignment on mobile"

examples.title: Amend the last commit (fix a mistake)
examples.description: You forgot to stage a file, or there's a typo in the message. --amend replaces the last commit entirely.
examples.code:
# Forgot to add a file:
git add forgotten-file.js
git commit --amend --no-edit
# The file is now part of the last commit

# Fix the commit message:
git commit --amend -m "Correct: add user login validation"

examples.title: Multi-line commit message
examples.description: For complex changes, write a detailed message with a summary line and explanation body.
examples.code:
git commit -m "Refactor auth middleware" -m "Extracted token validation into a separate module to improve testability. Updated all route handlers to use the new middleware. Added unit tests for edge cases (expired tokens, malformed headers)."

# Or let the editor handle it:
git commit
# (Your editor opens with a template for the message)

examples.title: Create an empty commit (trigger CI)
examples.description: Sometimes you need to trigger a CI/CD pipeline without any code changes. An empty commit is the cleanest way.
examples.code:
git commit --allow-empty -m "Trigger CI rebuild"
git push

commonMistakes.text: Never use `--amend` on commits that have already been pushed to a shared branch. Amending rewrites the commit hash, which breaks other people's history. Use `git revert` instead.
Vague messages like 'fix bug', 'update', or 'wip' make the history useless. Write messages that your future self (or teammates) can understand in 6 months: what changed, why, and what it affects.
If you commit and immediately realize the message is wrong, `git commit --amend -m "new message"` is safe as long as you haven't pushed yet. It's a very common and harmless operation.
Follow Conventional Commits (feat:, fix:, refactor:, docs:) for structured history. Tools like semantic-release can then auto-generate changelogs and version numbers.
